Frontline Trauma Specialists

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It's month end and trauma units are chaotic across the country. We spend the Saturday night a shift in Mitchells Plain trauma unit the busiest in metropole. The frontline of the health care system

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa Trauma specialists are world class and their expertise sought after internationally. In turn foreign trauma specialist are cueing up to spend time in South African trauma wards, nowhere in the world can you gain such a range of trauma medicine experience, with stab wounds to the heart and head trauma being the most frequent medical condition. But although South Africa’s Emergency Medicine specialists are globally sought after, their current working conditions may push them out of the local health sector.

Summary:
As South Africans we depend on these Trauma specialists to step in and save the day when disaster strikes our lives. But they are severely burnt out - COVID pushed them to the limit and since the pandemic has died down they have had no relief or time to recover. They are emotionally exhausted, feeling depersonalised and are losing their sense of personal achievement. They find themselves caught in a vicious cycle of work, sleep deprivation, and social isolation, with little time to recharge their batteries. The impact is depression, a range of health issues and something called moral injury. Burnout implies the person has failed by not managing stress better, moral injury indicates its the system that is failing and not the individual. The system in which they working forces them to behave in ways they cannot control and goes against the very reason they are doctors. There are not enough doctors, not enough beds and the patient load keeps increasing. Their shifts are so long they can no longer deliver the best quality of care and both the patient and the doctors and emergency staff are suffering.



Further information:
Their working conditions are extreme. 65% of their work is outside of ‘normal’ hours – versus 25% of work for most other disciplines being outside of normal working hours. They are constantly working under stress, treating up to 20 patients over an eight-to-twelve-hour shift. Besides the blood and guts and often-chaotic work pressure, each staffer reported daily verbal abuse and at least once-weekly physical abuse. One doctor said “It can be chaotic. In one hour, you can have a psychotic, aggressive and violent patient, then one with haemorrhagic shock about to die, then one in heart failure struggling to breathe, followed by a child with severe gastro and dehydration. Sometimes this can even be in the space of half an hour” And the patient they are seeing are sicker. TB and HIV programs were severely set back under COVID and so those patients are coming into trauma wards far sicker.

The doctors report being regularly bitten, kicked, punched, and urinated or vomited on while dealing with distressed patients suffering from a variety of life-threatening conditions that require quick-thinking and highly efficient triage.

Trauma specialist report suffering from compassion fatigue – when doctors get irritable with patients, every doctor’s nightmare of becoming abusive. The ‘short fuse’ is often a clue to impending burnout.

Month end is when things are at their most extreme, we will spend that time tracking the cases and the doctors getting their reflections on the job and then travel home with them to reflect their family circumstances and what they put on hold to care for what society throws at them

Driving
Abu “Today is Saturday evening I am doing a night shift at Mitchells Plain its about 7oclock now,
Couple of seconds of drama beeping “they shot” you- hello hello
Link- It’s month end and trauma centres around the country are bracing themselves for whatever society can throw at them, car accidents, stab victims, heart attacks. We are going to spend a Saturday night in Cape Towns busiest emergency centre - Mitchells Plain
Script: It’s an area notorious for drive-by shootings, gangs battles and violence… we’re anxious about what lies ahead
Script: Having started his community service at the beginning of the pandemic, Dr. Abubakr De Villiers has now qualified
Preparing for the sheer intensity of what’s to come, he pauses to listen to music for 10 minutes. PAUSE for additional UPSOUND
Barely through the door, he’s confronted by his first emergency: one of several assault victims he’ll see tonight.
upsound “ hello hello, what’s your name, what happened to you”
Script: Dr. Katya Evans, specialist emergency physician, is the consultant on call, providing backup to the team on duty.  The shift is just starting and already there are 80 waiting patients.

KAT “  Back lesions, assaults,  body pains 

Script: Within minutes the first medical emergency is wheeled in.

Upsound of groaning
KAT So this gentleman has had some neurological event, it’s either a stoke or a seizure…if he deteriorates further he will need a CT scan of his brain
Script: Dr. Priscilla Ohm is in charge tonight. Apart from Dr De Villiers, she’s working with a young and inexperienced team: two community service doctors and two visiting German students on duty for the first time. Despite that, she’s focussed and calm.
Priscilla: You have people that have been waiting about 6 hours, maybe 10 to 12 hours even in our unit, still daily sick still needing to be here, and that the patients that are getting rolled in are dying now. So I think that kind of balance, that continuous work and you feel like you're never catching up.
Upsound “I have a vein there- man coughing battling to breath”
Link: As the health system across the country takes strain people come to emergency centres like this one to access help, because they know nobody gets turned away. That means that the load on for emergency health workers is just getting heavier and heavier
Script: 5000 patients a month are treated here with trauma cases like knife and gunshot wounds accounting for just 15%. Still exhausted from dealing with the worst of Covid, emergency staff are now struggling with rising caseloads. 
Kat: So there's a lot of chronic diseases that were neglected and now the long term sort of complications of those, cancers with delayed diagnosis, picked up, you know, patients with very advanced or metastatic disease. And patients have got very complicated disease.
Script: : And many of them - the terminally ill - arrive here, taking their places alongside the trauma patients
Upsound “I am very sick”
Kat “We are worried you are very sick we will chat to your daughter as well but you are going to have to sleep in hospital ok. But not on this hard bed we are going to move you upstairs to a more comfortable bed in the ward ok
Script: Providing end-of-life care, in an emergency ward, is unexpected but something Dr. Evans is passionate about
Kat: If we see how many of our patients are terminally ill, we can care for them in a better way. provide them with medications or treatment to keep them comfortable in their last moments. How to provide dignity and respect and comfort in someone's dying moments in an environment that is not necessarily suited to that.
Upsound music
Script: It feels like we are on the edge of battlezone - blooded, punctured survivors wheeled in at high speed. 9 stab victims and counting, with the less critical propped up along the passage. And it’s only 12:30. PAUSE They’re assessed and patched up and quickly dispatched from the resuscitation area, making room for the next arrivals – who keep on coming.
Upsound” What happened to you- they stabbed you- ok, can we get him undressed he is very wet, groaning, There is a problem your lung is collapsed because they stabbed you in the back, I need to put a pipe into your chest so that your lung can expand again , ok?
Groaning, can I please have the blood pressure cuff, and general buzz
LINK These doctors have been on the go non stop, one patient every 7 minutes in this emergency centre here in Mitchells Plain, it’s unbelievable that their energy levels are as high as they are still after all these hours
Upsound Alarm beeping- oh no- change your gloves change your gloves
Script : This patient is deteriorating, he needs a cat scan and must be transferred as soon as they can get an ambulance. While they wait, amid the surrounding bustle, Dr Evans stops everything and ensures his mother has a moment with her son (LONGER PAUSE HERE)
Upsound music
LINK So these are not just medical professional they good humans, they understand that this is the patient’s worst moment and they are there to help them and that level of compassion, I actually have no words to describe it
Priscilla “People often picture doctors as being the lifesavers, but often people do die. And the aftercare with the family is also part of our job, but it's a highly neglected portion of our job, especially in the EC because someone dying right now is obviously takes priority over someone who has already passed away. So that kind of balance, I think, is a little bit challenging.
Upsound music
Script: As the night wares on, more inebriated assault victims arrive
Upsounds of man swearing, ok take him down there, Ahh fok off man. Are you onbeskoff…ahh fok off man
Script: Sister Maans head nurse for the emergency unit tonight intervenes.
Sister Maans “the worst happens on the weekend when patients are intoxicated, and their family also, so they push them in here demanding to be helped first, all the drunk patients wanting to be helped first forgetting we have other patients inside here, medical patients, ……
Kat: It's really tricky. We've had a lot of threats against our doctors. We've had physical assaults. We've had two doctors that have been very badly injured and assaulted and a lot of threats that they're going to be followed home after the end of shift.
SCRIPT: Something Sister Maans knows all too well, and it's not only violence she has to contend with
Sister Maans Our shift started at 7 and I have had to ventilate one patient and put them on Cpap so I need to go to the loo now, get some water to drink, I haven’t had a lunch break, …
Script: But the break is not to be, as she turns away the next stab victim is rushed in
Upsound
Link To the untrained eye like mine, it looks quite chaotic, treat one emergency and then move on to the next crisis, but it is very much like a pitstop in formula one, everyone has a role to play and time is of the essence, there is a system and it works
Music
Script:  It's 5.30 and there’s no letting up – fatigue inevitably sets in.
Priscilla:. It is a struggle but I think its a global struggle, all doctors work long shifts.
Upsound Groaning “Feel the bone I want you to push this way, I want you to feel if the the bone straight- groaning- sorry - great. Man sitting up in his bed screaming Priscilla no no no Kat- Security
Script: This stab victim appears to be re-living an earlier fight.
Swearing in Xhosa
Script There’s a two-year waiting list of foreign students wanting to volunteer here because we’re renowned for having the world’s toughest trauma units. Yet there’s still a shortage of emergency doctors because the job’s extreme pressure takes a toll – they’re burning out or leaving.
Claire” So what impact does it have on you having to work at this pace non-stop
Kat: it can break you down.18 20 20 A lot of our doctors are struggling with moral injury because you may be at times not providing the care that is in line with your principles and what is what you want to provide 18:20:55:11 …we have a lot more absenteeism from mental health, sick leave or for other reasons. It's very different to what it was a few years ago when it comes to staff burnout and depression.
Script: And the workforce is young, mostly community service doctors and newly qualified medical officers. 65% of their shifts are after hours- isolating them socially. No matter how dedicated - they only last a couple of years, leaving very few senior emergency medicine specialists in the system.
Abu I went through a bout of burnout towards the end of my community service….. I took off two months just to try and figure things out and find myself and try and recover from what had been a crazy year in the emergency unit during the peak of the COVID pandemic.
Script: Dawn finally breaks – it’s the home stretch and the nursing staff are changing shift 
Sister Maans “ Very very busy shift, we had lots of trauma patients about 11 stabs, most of our patients were intoxicated but the team work was there
Script: But the doctors have two and half hours to go and the paperwork is endless. This patient is still being patched up 8 hours later - An Xray shows his hand is fractured and Abu is concerned about the depression in his skull which will need a Cat scan.
Claire “Are you able to leave work here mentally when you walk away …and all the things we have seen this evening.
Abu “For the most part but there are those cases that stick with you and the ones you go home and you think about it for me its usually deaths involving young people , paediatric deaths or adolescent deaths
Script: This weekend 424 patients have come through this unit: 62% of them critical with 5 deaths. None of them on our shift.
Script: We emerge 14 hours later. The doctors make a point of going off shift together, never leaving anyone behind. As we leave one door, 5 critical patients are entering another. For now, though, it’s over -  but they’ll be back in just 10 hours to do it all again.
Priscilla driving” Funny how calm everything looks once the morning starts, like the night didn’t happen I think I was most appreciative that no one died yesterday, not everyday that you get a shift that you don’t have to break bad news, so it was a pretty good shift.

As we leave one door, 5 critical patients are entering another. For now, though, it’s over - but they’ll be back in just 10 hours to do it all again. Priscilla driving” Funny how calm everything looks once the morning starts, like the night didn’t happen I think I was most appreciative that no one died yesterday, not everyday that you get a shift that you don’t have to break bad news, so it was a pretty good shift.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It's month end and trauma units are chaotic across the country. We spend the Saturday night a shift in Mitchells Plain trauma unit the busiest in metropole. The frontline of the health care system
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africa Trauma specialists are world class and their expertise sought after internationally. In turn foreign trauma specialist are cueing up to spend time in South African trauma wards, nowhere in the world can you gain such a range of trauma medicine experience, with stab wounds to the heart and head trauma being the most frequent medical condition. But although South Africa’s Emergency Medicine specialists are globally sought after, their current working conditions may push them out of the local health sector.
metadata.Summary: As South Africans we depend on these Trauma specialists to step in and save the day when disaster strikes our lives. But they are severely burnt out - COVID pushed them to the limit and since the pandemic has died down they have had no relief or time to recover. They are emotionally exhausted, feeling depersonalised and are losing their sense of personal achievement. They find themselves caught in a vicious cycle of work, sleep deprivation, and social isolation, with little time to recharge their batteries. The impact is depression, a range of health issues and something called moral injury. Burnout implies the person has failed by not managing stress better, moral injury indicates its the system that is failing and not the individual. The system in which they working forces them to behave in ways they cannot control and goes against the very reason they are doctors. There are not enough doctors, not enough beds and the patient load keeps increasing. Their shifts are so long they can no longer deliver the best quality of care and both the patient and the doctors and emergency staff are suffering.
metadata.Further information: Their working conditions are extreme. 65% of their work is outside of ‘normal’ hours – versus 25% of work for most other disciplines being outside of normal working hours. They are constantly working under stress, treating up to 20 patients over an eight-to-twelve-hour shift. Besides the blood and guts and often-chaotic work pressure, each staffer reported daily verbal abuse and at least once-weekly physical abuse. One doctor said “It can be chaotic. In one hour, you can have a psychotic, aggressive and violent patient, then one with haemorrhagic shock about to die, then one in heart failure struggling to breathe, followed by a child with severe gastro and dehydration. Sometimes this can even be in the space of half an hour” And the patient they are seeing are sicker. TB and HIV programs were severely set back under COVID and so those patients are coming into trauma wards far sicker. The doctors report being regularly bitten, kicked, punched, and urinated or vomited on while dealing with distressed patients suffering from a variety of life-threatening conditions that require quick-thinking and highly efficient triage. Trauma specialist report suffering from compassion fatigue – when doctors get irritable with patients, every doctor’s nightmare of becoming abusive. The ‘short fuse’ is often a clue to impending burnout. Month end is when things are at their most extreme, we will spend that time tracking the cases and the doctors getting their reflections on the job and then travel home with them to reflect their family circumstances and what they put on hold to care for what society throws at them
